group.title: Formal collocations
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To have influence and be taken seriously by others.
examples: Her opinion {carries weight} with the board.
wrong: His views carry weight, so nobody pays any attention to them.

words.meaning: To arrive at an agreement that everyone in a group accepts.
examples: After hours of debate, the board {reached a consensus}.
wrong: They reached a consensus, so nobody agreed with anyone.

words.meaning: To say formally that you are worried about something.
examples: Parents {raised concerns} about the new timetable.
wrong: He raised concerns by saying he was completely happy.

words.meaning: To point out clearly how two things are different.
examples: The report {draws a distinction} between weather and climate.
wrong: She drew a distinction by saying the two ideas were exactly the same.

words.meaning: To be the person who must answer for something.
examples: The company {bears responsibility} for the delay.
wrong: She bears responsibility, so the problem has nothing to do with her.

words.meaning: To have all the qualities that are required.
examples: Only three applicants {met the criteria}.
wrong: He met the criteria, so he was rejected for not qualifying.

words.meaning: To grow stronger and develop faster over time.
examples: The campaign {gained momentum} as more people joined.
wrong: The movement gained momentum and slowly faded away.

words.meaning: To have and use power over people or events.
examples: Large banks {wield influence} over national policy.
wrong: The tiny club wields influence, so nobody listens to it.

words.meaning: To be more important and dealt with first.
examples: Safety must {take precedence} over speed.
wrong: Safety takes precedence, so we deal with it last.

words.meaning: To show that something is especially important.
examples: The school {places emphasis on} reading.
wrong: The coach placed emphasis on fitness by never mentioning it.

words.meaning: To cause something to happen or begin.
examples: The new policy {gave rise to} protests.
wrong: The decision gave rise to nothing; it caused many changes.

words.meaning: To help explain something or make it clearer.
examples: The letters {shed light on} her early life.
wrong: The study shed light on the problem, making it even more confusing.

words.meaning: To start being officially used, as a law or rule does.
examples: The new rules {come into force} in January.
wrong: The law came into force, so nobody has to follow it.

words.meaning: To make an official complaint to a person or organization.
examples: She {lodged a complaint} with the city council.
wrong: He lodged a complaint to say how pleased he was.

words.meaning: To have to pay money because of something you did.
examples: Late cancellations may {incur costs} for the guest.
wrong: We incurred costs, so we didn’t have to pay anything.

words.meaning: To be examined closely and critically by others.
examples: The company’s accounts have {come under scrutiny}.
wrong: The plan came under scrutiny, so nobody looked at it closely.

words.meaning: To do what you have a duty or promise to do.
examples: The firm {fulfilled its obligations} under the contract.
wrong: He fulfilled his obligation by ignoring his duty.

words.meaning: To officially allow someone to do something.
examples: The council {granted permission} for the new building.
wrong: They granted permission by refusing every request.

words.meaning: To give up something to reach an agreement.
examples: Both sides had to {make concessions} to end the strike.
wrong: She made a concession by refusing to give up anything.

words.meaning: To do something that will be used as an example for future cases.
examples: The ruling could {set a precedent} for similar cases.
wrong: The decision set a precedent, so it will never affect later cases.

words.meaning: To say publicly that you disagree with something.
examples: Several members {voiced objections} to the plan.
wrong: He voiced an objection by saying he fully agreed.

words.meaning: To praise and show respect for someone publicly.
examples: The speaker {paid tribute to} the volunteers.
wrong: She paid tribute to her teacher by insulting him on stage.

words.meaning: To think that something matters a lot.
examples: Our company {attaches importance to} customer service.
wrong: They attach importance to safety, so they ignore it.

words.meaning: To be careful in a risky situation.
examples: Drivers should {exercise caution} on icy roads.
wrong: He exercised caution by driving as fast as he could.

words.meaning: To make someone accept responsibility for what they did.
examples: Voters will {hold the government accountable}.
wrong: They held him accountable by pretending the mistake never happened.

words.meaning: To act quickly to use a good chance.
examples: She {seized the opportunity} to study abroad.
wrong: He seized the opportunity by letting it pass.

words.meaning: To say formally that you have some doubts about something.
examples: Several experts {expressed reservations} about the plan.
wrong: He expressed reservations by saying he had no doubts at all.

words.meaning: To reduce the difference between two things or groups.
examples: The program aims to {bridge the gap} between rich and poor.
wrong: The policy bridged the gap by making the difference much bigger.

words.meaning: To be in a situation where something bad could happen.
examples: If you skip class, you {run the risk of} failing.
wrong: He ran the risk of failing, so failure was impossible.

words.meaning: A clear and noticeable change for the better.
examples: There has been {a marked improvement} in her grades.
wrong: There was a marked improvement, so things got worse.

words.meaning: Another option that could really work.
examples: Solar power is now {a viable alternative} to coal.
wrong: It’s a viable alternative, so it could never work.

words.meaning: A personal reason, often about money, for wanting something to happen.
examples: Builders have {a vested interest} in the new road.
wrong: He has a vested interest, so the result means nothing to him.

words.meaning: A result that is certain before something even happens.
examples: The election result was {a foregone conclusion}.
wrong: The match was a foregone conclusion, so nobody could predict who would win.

words.meaning: Happening after and because of an event.
examples: Prices rose {in the wake of} the storm.
wrong: The rules changed in the wake of the scandal, two years before it happened.

words.meaning: Something that must be dealt with very quickly.
examples: The repairs should be done as {a matter of urgency}.
wrong: It’s a matter of urgency, so we can deal with it next year.

words.meaning: Approval from many people in many places.
examples: The plan has {widespread support} among residents.
wrong: The idea had widespread support, as almost nobody liked it.

words.meaning: The ability to make sensible, good decisions.
examples: A good manager needs {sound judgment}.
wrong: She showed sound judgment by making one foolish choice after another.

words.meaning: To give help or agreement to a person or idea.
examples: Several groups {lent support} to the campaign.
wrong: He lent support to the plan by voting against it.

words.meaning: To make people feel less worried.
examples: The minister tried to {allay fears} about the virus.
wrong: His calm words allayed fears and made everyone panic.

words.meaning: A sudden and large fall in amount or quality.
examples: There was {a sharp decline} in sales last year.
wrong: Sales showed a sharp decline, rising quickly to a record.
